section_title: What can the finest ship do when the east wind breaks it?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 25 The ships of Tarshish carried your merchandise. And you were filled with heavy cargo in the heart of the sea. 26 Your oarsmen have brought you onto the high seas, but the east wind will shatter you in the heart of the sea. 27 Your wealth, wares, and merchandise, your sailors, captains, and shipwrights, your merchants and all the warriors within you, with all the other people on board, will sink into the heart of the sea on the day of your downfall.

context_lines: The trading ships have filled Tyre with heavy cargo. The poem then brings the magnificent vessel onto the high seas, where an east wind shatters it.
Everything gathered into the city falls together: wealth, wares, crew, merchants, warriors and the other people on board. The very fullness that displayed success cannot keep the ship afloat.
The picture concerns Tyre’s overthrow. The poem uses a catastrophe at sea to make the collapse of the city and its supporting world visible.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/ezekiel/27.htm) understands the rowers as rulers and advisers, and the east wind as the king of Babylon with his army. [Cambridge](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/ezekiel/27.htm) is more cautious about how far the image identifies particular actions by Tyre’s leaders, emphasizing the force that breaks the vessel beyond human control.

[Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/27.htm) reads the fall as a warning about resting hope in created powers that can themselves collapse. The difference in detail does not alter the poem’s devastating reversal of confidence.
god_plan_lines: The wider biblical answer to fragile security is a foundation God supplies. [First Peter 2:4–8](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/2.htm) applies Isaiah’s promise of a chosen cornerstone to Christ and describes believers being built into a spiritual house through Him.

This is a connection between themes, not a claim that Tyre’s ship secretly represents the church. Ezekiel exposes confidence that cannot survive the downfall of its object. Peter directs people to the living Christ, the stone chosen by God, in whom those who believe will not be put to shame.
